ch42.note: Tao Zhu (陶铸, 1908–1969), a Communist political officer—here director of a Northeast field-army political department—who rose after 1949 to the top ranks of the Party and was then purged and hounded to death in the Cultural Revolution.

Liu Jin (刘瑾) was a notoriously corrupt and powerful eunuch of the Ming Zhengde reign; 'The Famen Temple' is the Peking-opera courtroom drama in which he presides over a murder case, sung as a jing or painted-face role.

ch42.anchor: covenant made beneath the city walls
ch42.note: A 'covenant beneath the walls' (城下之盟) is the classical term for a humiliating surrender wrung from a besieged city—applied here, with its full sting, to Fu Zuoyi's negotiated handover of Beiping.

Tang Enbo (汤恩伯, 1898–1954), a senior Nationalist general who commanded the doomed defense of Shanghai in 1949 and then the outlying islands—the headquarters that took Chen's unit up for the Shanghai fighting.

The Minnan or Hokkien tongue of southern Fujian, spoken also in Penghu and across much of Taiwan and not mutually intelligible with Mandarin—which is why a mainland northerner had to learn it to get by among the islanders.

Nemoto Hiroshi (根本博, 1891–1966), a former Japanese lieutenant general who slipped secretly to Taiwan in late 1949 and served as a personal adviser to Tang Enbo, helping direct the Nationalist defense of Kinmen. His role was so awkward, in those anti-Japanese years, that the Republic of China acknowledged it only in 2009.

CAT was Civil Air Transport, the airline founded after the war by Claire Chennault of Flying Tigers fame; it flew the Nationalists' men and freight through the collapse and was later tied to the American CIA.
